title: Epithelium & Glands
summary: Master the first tissue type: how epithelia are classified, held together, specialized and renewed.

lessons.title: Classifying Epithelia by Layers & Shape

levels.kid:
Your body is covered and lined with sheets of cells packed tightly together, like tiles on a bathroom floor. These sheets are called **epithelium**. They cover your skin and line your mouth, stomach and blood vessels.

Scientists name each sheet with two clues:
- **How many layers?** One layer is called simple. Many layers stacked up is called stratified.
- **What shape are the top cells?** Flat like pancakes (squamous), square like dice (cuboidal), or tall like columns (columnar).

Thin, flat sheets are great where things need to pass through easily, like in your lungs. Thick, stacked sheets are great where things rub a lot, like your skin. The shape and layers match the job!
levels.hs:
**Epithelium** is a tissue made of cells packed closely together in sheets. It covers body surfaces, lines hollow organs and tubes, and forms glands. It sits on a thin supporting layer called the **basement membrane** and has no blood vessels of its own, so it gets nutrients by diffusion from the tissue underneath.

Histologists name an epithelium using two features:
- **Number of layers.** **Simple** means one layer of cells. **Stratified** means two or more layers.
- **Shape of the cells.** **Squamous** cells are flat, **cuboidal** cells are about as tall as they are wide, and **columnar** cells are taller than they are wide.

For stratified epithelium, the name comes from the shape of the *top* (surface) layer only. For example, skin is **stratified squamous**, even though its deepest cells are cuboidal or columnar.

Structure follows function:
- **Simple squamous** lines blood vessels and the air sacs (alveoli) of the lungs, where gases must diffuse quickly.
- **Simple cuboidal** lines kidney tubules and small gland ducts, which absorb and secrete.
- **Simple columnar** lines the stomach and intestines, where cells absorb food and make mucus.
- **Stratified squamous** protects areas that get rubbed, like the esophagus and skin.

A real example: a pathologist looking at a biopsy from the esophagus expects stratified squamous cells. Finding columnar cells there instead is a warning sign of disease.
levels.college:
Epithelia are classified by two independent criteria: the **number of cell layers** and the **shape of the most superficial cells**. Two further categories, pseudostratified and transitional, do not fit cleanly and are named separately.

**Simple epithelia (one layer, every cell touches the basement membrane)**
- **Simple squamous**: flattened cells with bulging nuclei. Called **endothelium** when lining vessels and the heart, **mesothelium** when lining the pleural, pericardial and peritoneal cavities. Also lines alveoli and Bowman's capsule (parietal layer). Built for diffusion and filtration.
- **Simple cuboidal**: round central nuclei; kidney tubules, thyroid follicles, small ducts, ovarian surface. Secretion and absorption.
- **Simple columnar**: oval basal nuclei, often with goblet cells; stomach, small and large intestine, gallbladder, uterine tube.

**Pseudostratified columnar**: one layer, but nuclei sit at different heights and not every cell reaches the lumen, so it *looks* stratified. All cells contact the basement membrane. Classic site: the trachea and bronchi (ciliated, with goblet cells, the "respiratory epithelium").

**Stratified epithelia (two or more layers, named by the surface layer)**
- **Stratified squamous keratinized**: epidermis; surface cells are dead and filled with keratin.
- **Stratified squamous nonkeratinized**: oral cavity, esophagus, vagina, cornea; surface cells keep nuclei and stay moist.
- **Stratified cuboidal** and **stratified columnar**: rare; larger ducts of sweat and salivary glands, parts of the male urethra, conjunctiva.

**Transitional epithelium (urothelium)**: lines the renal pelvis, ureters, bladder and proximal urethra. Large dome-shaped **umbrella cells** on the surface flatten when the bladder stretches, so the number of visible layers seems to shrink.

Practical reading tip: to tell simple from stratified, trace cells from the basement membrane to the lumen. To judge shape, look at the nucleus. Flat nuclei suggest squamous, round nuclei cuboidal, and elongated nuclei columnar.
levels.phd:
The layers-by-shape scheme is a morphological convention dating to 19th-century microscopy. It is descriptively powerful but biologically shallow: it groups tissues with unrelated origins and functions. Epithelia arise from all three germ layers. Epidermis and corneal epithelium come from ectoderm, the gut lining from endoderm, and endothelium, mesothelium and the kidney tubules from mesoderm. Whether endothelium and mesothelium count as "true" epithelia is debated, because they derive from mesenchyme and express vimentin alongside or instead of the keratins typical of epithelia.

**Keratin expression as molecular classification.** Keratins are type I (acidic, K9 to K28) and type II (basic, K1 to K8) intermediate filaments that pair as heterodimers. Expression tracks the morphological categories closely:
- Simple epithelia express **K8/K18**, often with K7, K19 or K20.
- Basal cells of stratified epithelia express **K5/K14**.
- Suprabasal keratinizing epidermis switches to **K1/K10**. Nonkeratinized mucosa such as esophagus and cornea uses **K4/K13** and **K3/K12** respectively.
Mutations in K5/K14 cause epidermolysis bullosa simplex, in which basal cells fragment under mechanical stress. This is direct genetic evidence that keratins provide the mechanical resilience suited to stratified epithelia.

**Pseudostratification.** In developing neuroepithelium, interkinetic nuclear migration moves nuclei apically for mitosis and basally for S phase, producing a pseudostratified look. Adult airway pseudostratification instead reflects distinct cell types: basal stem cells sit low, while columnar ciliated and secretory cells reach the lumen.

**Urothelium.** Umbrella cells are often binucleate or polyploid. Their apical membrane is covered with **uroplakin** plaques (UPIa, Ib, II, IIIa) that form an asymmetric unit membrane. Discoid and fusiform vesicles add membrane to the surface during filling and retrieve it during voiding, so the cells can change surface area without tearing.

**Polarity.** Apical-basal polarity is set up by the Crumbs, Par (Par3/Par6/aPKC) and Scribble complexes. Polarity is a defining epithelial property that the shape-and-layer label leaves out.
levels.expert:
For the practising pathologist, the layers-and-shape vocabulary is mainly a tool for recognizing epithelium in the wrong place or of the wrong type.

**Diagnostic recognition.**
- **Barrett esophagus**: columnar epithelium with goblet cells (intestinal metaplasia) replaces stratified squamous in the distal esophagus. It is the precursor lesion for esophageal adenocarcinoma.
- **Squamous metaplasia of the bronchus** in smokers converts pseudostratified ciliated epithelium to stratified squamous. This trades mucociliary clearance for resistance to irritation and sets the stage for squamous cell carcinoma.
- The **cervical transformation zone**, where columnar epithelium meets ectocervical squamous epithelium, is where HPV-driven neoplasia arises. This is why cervical screening samples that zone.

**Tangential sectioning.** This is a major pitfall. An oblique cut through simple columnar or pseudostratified epithelium can mimic stratification, and can even mimic invasion in colonic polyps. Always find a perpendicular region where the basement membrane runs straight.

**Immunohistochemistry extends morphology.** In carcinoma of unknown primary, the **CK7/CK20** pattern narrows the origin. CK7−/CK20+ points to colorectal origin, CK7+/CK20− to lung or breast, and CK7+/CK20+ to urothelial or pancreaticobiliary origin. **p63** and **CK5/6** mark squamous and basal differentiation and help separate squamous cell carcinoma from adenocarcinoma in lung biopsies, which guides therapy. **GATA3** and uroplakin II support urothelial origin.

**Neurosurgical relevance.** Ependyma is a simple cuboidal-to-columnar ciliated lining of the ventricles that lacks a true basement membrane. Choroid plexus epithelium is simple cuboidal, forms the blood-CSF barrier, and gives rise to choroid plexus papillomas. Craniopharyngiomas show stratified squamous differentiation. The adamantinomatous type carries CTNNB1 mutations, and the papillary type carries BRAF V600E.

**Open questions.** Single-cell atlases (for example the Human Cell Atlas airway data) reveal rare types such as **ionocytes**, which are rich in CFTR, and tuft cells that classical categories never captured. This prompts the question of whether shape-based labels should give way to transcriptional cell-state taxonomies, or simply be layered beneath them.

keyPoints: Epithelia are named by number of layers (simple vs stratified) and cell shape
Shapes: squamous (flat), cuboidal, columnar (tall)
Stratified epithelia are named by the shape of the surface layer
Pseudostratified looks layered, but every cell touches the basement membrane
Transitional epithelium (urothelium) stretches, with umbrella cells on the surface
Form matches function: thin for diffusion, stacked for protection

test.q: Which epithelium lines the lung alveoli to allow fast gas diffusion?
test.explain: A single layer of flat cells gives the shortest diffusion distance. Columnar or stratified epithelia would be too thick.

test.q: A stratified epithelium is named according to the shape of its:
test.explain: The superficial layer sets the name. Skin is stratified squamous even though its basal cells are cuboidal to columnar.

test.q: What makes pseudostratified epithelium only 'falsely' stratified?
choices: It has no basement membrane beneath it
Its surface is covered by keratin layers
Each cell sits on the basement membrane
Its top cells are flattened like scales
test.explain: Nuclei sit at different heights, but it is truly one layer because every cell rests on the basement membrane.

test.q: Where is ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium classically found?
test.explain: The trachea and bronchi carry respiratory epithelium. The esophagus is stratified squamous and the bladder is transitional.

test.q: Which epithelium lines the urinary bladder?
test.explain: Transitional epithelium (urothelium), with dome-shaped umbrella cells, stretches as the bladder fills.

test.q: Kidney tubules and thyroid follicles are lined mainly by:
test.explain: Cube-shaped cells with round central nuclei line these absorptive and secretory structures.

test.q: How does the esophagus lining differ from the epidermis?
test.explain: Both are stratified squamous, but the esophagus is nonkeratinized and moist, while the epidermis is keratinized.

test.q: A nucleus that is oval and elongated, placed near the base of a tall cell, suggests a cell that is:
test.explain: Nuclear shape hints at cell shape. Elongated nuclei suggest columnar cells, flat nuclei squamous, and round nuclei cuboidal.

test.q: Simple squamous epithelium lining blood vessels is called:
test.explain: Endothelium lines vessels and the heart. Mesothelium lines body cavities such as the pleura and peritoneum.

test.q: What term describes an epithelium made of two or more cell layers?
test.explain: Stratified means layered. A single layer is called simple.

test.q: Flat, pancake-like epithelial cells are described as ___.
test.explain: Squamous means scale-like or flat.

test.q: What is the name for the large dome-shaped surface cells of transitional epithelium?
test.explain: Umbrella cells flatten as the bladder stretches and protect it from urine.

kidTest.q: What is epithelium?
choices: A kind of bone inside your arm
Cell sheets that cover your body
A liquid that flows in your blood
kidTest.explain: Epithelium is made of tightly packed cell sheets, like tiles.

kidTest.q: What does 'simple' mean for epithelium?
kidTest.explain: Simple means one layer. Stratified means many layers.

kidTest.q: Which shape are columnar cells?
kidTest.explain: Columnar cells are tall, like the columns of a building.

kidTest.q: Why is skin made of many stacked layers?
choices: To let air pass through fast
kidTest.explain: Thick, stacked layers protect places that get rubbed a lot.

kidTest.q: Very flat cells are called s _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Squamous cells are flat like pancakes.

advancedTest.q: A lung biopsy tumor is p63-positive and CK5/6-positive. Which conclusion is best supported?
choices: Squamous differentiation of the tumor cells
Adenocarcinoma arising from simple columnar epithelium
Urothelial origin metastatic to the lung
Endothelial origin from vessel lining cells
advancedTest.explain: p63 and CK5/6 mark basal and squamous differentiation, which separates squamous cell carcinoma from adenocarcinoma. GATA3 and uroplakin would point to urothelial origin.

advancedTest.q: A colonic polyp section seems to show stratified, multilayered glands. What should a careful reader check first?
choices: Whether the cells are expressing K1 and K10
Whether tangential cutting is mimicking the layering
Whether keratin layers cover the surface cells
Whether the umbrella cells are binucleate
advancedTest.explain: An oblique section through simple columnar epithelium can mimic stratification or even invasion. A perpendicular region with a straight basement membrane settles it.

advancedTest.q: Mutations in K5/K14 cause blistering from basal cell fragility. What does this best show?
choices: Simple epithelia rely mainly on K5/K14 for strength
Basement membranes are built from keratin fibers
Keratin loss converts squamous cells to columnar
Keratins give stratified epithelia mechanical resilience
advancedTest.explain: K5/K14 are basal keratins of stratified epithelia. Their failure under mechanical stress shows that keratins supply structural toughness. Simple epithelia use K8/K18 instead.

advancedTest.q: Why is calling endothelium a 'true' epithelium debated?
choices: It is a stratified tissue lacking polarity
It lacks any contact with a basal lamina
It derives from the ectoderm like epidermis
It is mesenchymal in origin and expresses vimentin
advancedTest.explain: Endothelium is simple squamous in form, but it comes from mesenchyme and expresses vimentin rather than typical keratins. Its morphology and lineage therefore point in different directions.

lessons.title: Apical Specializations: Microvilli, Cilia & Stereocilia

levels.kid:
The cells that line the inside of your body have a top side that faces open space, like the inside of your gut or your airways. That top side is called the **apical** side, and it often has tiny tools sticking out of it.

- **Microvilli** are like the soft loops on a fluffy towel. They make the surface much bigger, so your gut can soak up more food.
- **Cilia** are like tiny oars that wave together. In your airways they sweep sticky mucus and dust up toward your throat.
- **Stereocilia** are long, stiff fingers. In your ear they bend when sound arrives, and that helps you hear.

You need a microscope to see them, because they are super small!
levels.hs:
Epithelial cells have a top surface facing a lumen (an open space) called the **apical** surface. Many of them build special structures there, each suited to a job.

- **Microvilli** are short, finger-like projections about 1 micrometer tall. They are held up by a bundle of **actin** filaments. Thousands packed together form the **brush border** of the small intestine, which greatly increases the surface area for absorbing nutrients. Under a light microscope it looks like a fuzzy pink stripe on top of the cells.
- **Cilia** are longer, about 5-10 micrometers. They are built from **microtubules** and can beat back and forth. In the trachea, cilia beat in coordinated waves to push mucus toward the throat. This is called the **mucociliary escalator**.
- **Stereocilia** are unusually long microvilli. Despite the name, they do not move on their own and contain actin, not microtubules. They are found in the epididymis, where they help absorb fluid, and in the inner ear, where they detect vibration.

A real example: smoking paralyzes and damages airway cilia. Mucus then builds up, which is one reason smokers cough so much.

Tip for slides: a brush border looks fuzzy and tight, while cilia look like taller, distinct hairs sitting on a dark line of **basal bodies**.
levels.college:
Apical specializations are classified by their cytoskeletal core, which predicts whether they can move.

**Microvilli (actin-based, non-motile)**
- Around 1 μm tall and 0.1 μm wide. The core holds 20-30 parallel actin filaments cross-linked by **villin** and **fimbrin**, and is anchored laterally to the membrane by **myosin I**.
- The rootlets insert into the **terminal web**, a horizontal actin-spectrin meshwork just below the apex.
- Enterocytes carry around 3,000 each, forming the striated (brush) border. The kidney's proximal tubule has a similar brush border. Together with folds and villi, they amplify intestinal absorptive area many-fold.
- The glycocalyx covering them anchors digestive enzymes such as lactase and sucrase-isomaltase.

**Cilia (microtubule-based)**
- The **axoneme** has a **9+2** arrangement: nine outer doublet microtubules around a central pair.
- **Dynein** arms on the doublets use ATP to slide adjacent doublets past one another. **Nexin** links resist the sliding, so the force bends the cilium into a fast effective stroke followed by a slower recovery stroke.
- Each cilium grows from a **basal body**, which has 9 triplets and no central pair, like a centriole.
- Locations: respiratory epithelium (pseudostratified ciliated columnar), uterine tube, ependyma.
- **Primary cilia** are solitary, 9+0, usually non-motile sensory organelles found on most cells.

**Stereocilia (actin-based, non-motile)**
- These are very long microvilli, up to about 120 μm in the epididymis, often branched and clumped.
- In the epididymis and ductus deferens they serve absorption.
- Cochlear and vestibular hair cells carry stereocilia arranged in graded rows like a staircase. These act as mechanosensors.

On H&E, cilia sit on a dark band of basal bodies. Microvilli form a thin refractile border with no such band.
levels.phd:
**Microvillar length control.** Brush-border microvilli are remarkably uniform in length, which reflects a balance between actin polymerization at the tip and treadmilling toward the base. Two classes of protein shape them. **Protocadherin-24 and CDHR5** form intermicrovillar adhesion links that pack the brush border into a hexagonal array. **Myosin VIIb**, harmonin and ANKS4B make up the intermicrovillar adhesion complex that holds those links in place. Myosin Ia drives membrane vesicles off microvillar tips into the lumen. **Ezrin**, activated by phosphorylation, tethers the membrane to the actin core.

**Axonemal mechanics.** Outer dynein arms (ODA) control beat frequency, while inner dynein arms (IDA) shape the waveform. Radial spokes and the central-pair apparatus regulate which dyneins are active, so the doublets on one side are engaged at any moment. Bending arises because nexin-dynein regulatory complexes turn sliding into curvature. Airway cilia beat at roughly 10-20 Hz. Neighbouring cilia fall into **metachronal waves** that emerge from hydrodynamic coupling. The cilia move a periciliary liquid layer under the mucus; the **gel-on-brush** model (Button et al., 2012) explains how membrane-tethered mucins keep this layer from collapsing.

**Ciliogenesis.** Multiciliated cells amplify centrioles through **deuterosomes**, driven by the regulators MCIDAS and FOXJ1, producing about 200-300 basal bodies per cell. Axonemes are built by **intraflagellar transport (IFT)**: kinesin-2 carries IFT-B particles toward the tip (anterograde), and dynein-2 carries IFT-A particles back (retrograde). The transition zone acts as a diffusion barrier that sorts which proteins enter the cilium.

**Hair-cell stereocilia.** These rely on parallel actin bundles cross-linked by espin, plastin and fascin-2. **Tip links** are made of cadherin-23 (upper end) and protocadherin-15 (lower end). Deflection toward the tallest row opens the MET channel, whose core components are **TMC1/2**, within microseconds. Length is regulated by myosin XVa together with whirlin and by myosin IIIa/b with espin-1. Stereociliary actin turns over unusually slowly, which may help explain why hair-cell damage is permanent.

The 9+0 versus 9+2 distinction does not map neatly onto motility. Nodal cilia are 9+0 yet motile, and they generate the leftward flow that sets left-right body asymmetry.
levels.expert:
**Primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD).** PCD is mostly autosomal recessive and has been linked to more than 50 genes, including DNAH5, DNAI1, CCDC39/40 and RSPH genes. It causes neonatal respiratory distress, chronic wet cough, bronchiectasis, sinusitis, otitis and subfertility. About half of patients have **situs inversus** (Kartagener syndrome) because nodal flow fails and left-right patterning becomes random.

Diagnosis is a practical pitfall. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) appears normal in roughly 30% of cases, for example with DNAH11 or RSPH variants. Current guidelines therefore combine nasal nitric oxide, high-speed video microscopy, immunofluorescence for dynein proteins, and genetic panels. Secondary dyskinesia after a viral infection mimics PCD, so samples should be repeated or grown in culture before a diagnosis is made.

Male infertility in PCD also involves the flagellar axoneme of the sperm tail. The flagellum is related to the cilium but is not the same: it has accessory structures such as outer dense fibers.

**Primary-cilium ciliopathies.** Defects in IFT or the transition zone cause:
- polycystic kidney disease (polycystin-1/2 sit on cilia);
- Joubert syndrome, with the **molar tooth sign** on MRI;
- Meckel-Gruber and Bardet-Biedl syndromes.

For neurosurgery, primary cilia transduce **Sonic hedgehog** signalling through Smoothened and the GLI factors. SHH-subgroup medulloblastoma depends on this ciliary signalling, and some tumours with downstream mutations escape Smoothened inhibitors such as vismodegib. Ependymal cilia drive local CSF flow, and mouse ependymal ciliary defects cause hydrocephalus, although the human link is weaker.

**Microvillus pathology.**
- **Microvillus inclusion disease** (MYO5B) causes intractable congenital diarrhea, with brush-border loss and intracytoplasmic microvillus-lined inclusions visible on TEM or with CD10 staining.
- In **celiac disease**, the brush border is lost alongside villous atrophy.
- CD10 or villin staining marks intestinal-type differentiation in tumour pathology.

**Hearing.** Mutations affecting tip-link and stereocilia proteins (CDH23, PCDH15, MYO7A, TMC1) cause syndromic Usher deafness and nonsyndromic deafness. Ototoxic aminoglycosides enter hair cells partly through MET channels. Gene therapy using AAV-delivered OTOF has restored hearing in children (2024 trials), though OTOF acts at the synapse rather than the stereocilia.

Open questions include how motile ciliary beating is coordinated across tissues, and whether regenerating stereocilia could make hair-cell replacement functional.

keyPoints: Apical specializations face the lumen and suit each epithelium's job
Microvilli: short actin cores (villin, fimbrin) forming the brush border for absorption
Cilia: 9+2 microtubule axoneme moved by dynein, growing from basal bodies
Stereocilia: long non-motile microvilli in epididymis and inner ear hair cells
Mucociliary escalator clears airway mucus; failure occurs in PCD/Kartagener
Primary cilia (9+0) are sensory and carry Hedgehog signalling

test.q: What forms the structural core of a microvillus?
test.explain: Microvilli contain 20-30 parallel actin filaments. Microtubules are the core of cilia, not microvilli.

test.q: The brush border of the small intestine mainly serves to:
test.explain: Densely packed microvilli amplify the surface area available for absorbing nutrients.

test.q: A motile cilium's axoneme has which arrangement?
choices: Nine doublets around a central pair
test.explain: Motile cilia are 9+2. Nine triplets describes the basal body, and 9+0 describes primary cilia.

test.q: Which motor protein powers ciliary bending?
test.explain: Dynein arms use ATP to slide adjacent doublets past one another. Villin is an actin cross-linker in microvilli.

test.q: Stereocilia differ from cilia because stereocilia:
test.explain: Despite their name, stereocilia are long microvilli with actin cores that do not beat.

test.q: Where would you expect to find stereocilia?
test.explain: Stereocilia line the epididymis and inner-ear hair cells. The trachea and uterine tube carry motile cilia.

test.q: On an H&E slide, which feature suggests cilia rather than microvilli?
choices: A dark band of basal bodies
test.explain: Cilia sit on a dark line of basal bodies. Microvilli form a thin border with no such band.

test.q: Why does smoking cause mucus to build up in the airways?
test.explain: Smoke paralyzes and damages cilia, so the mucociliary escalator fails to clear mucus.

test.q: Into what structure do microvillar actin rootlets anchor?
test.explain: The terminal web is an actin-spectrin meshwork just below the apex where microvillar rootlets insert.

test.q: What is the name of the centriole-like structure from which each cilium grows?
test.explain: Basal bodies have nine triplets and template the ciliary axoneme.

test.q: Coordinated airway cilia push mucus upward in the mucociliary ___.
test.explain: The mucociliary escalator moves trapped particles toward the throat.

test.q: Which actin-bundling protein, named for the villi, cross-links filaments in microvilli?
test.explain: Villin and fimbrin bundle the actin core of microvilli.

kidTest.q: What do microvilli in your gut help with?
kidTest.explain: They make the gut surface bigger, so it can absorb more food.

kidTest.q: What do cilia in your airways do?
kidTest.explain: Cilia wave like oars to move sticky mucus and dust out of your airways.

kidTest.q: Where do stereocilia help you hear?
kidTest.explain: Stereocilia in the inner ear bend when sound arrives.

kidTest.q: Why do we need a microscope to see these parts?
kidTest.explain: They are far too small to see with your eyes alone.

kidTest.q: Tiny waving hairs that act like oars are called c _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Cilia beat together like rowers' oars.

advancedTest.q: A child has chronic wet cough, sinusitis and situs inversus, but ciliary TEM looks normal. The best interpretation is:
choices: Situs inversus here most likely reflects a primary-cilium Hedgehog defect
PCD is ruled out because the axoneme ultrastructure is normal
The findings point to microvillus inclusion disease instead
PCD is still possible, since some genotypes such as DNAH11 show normal TEM
advancedTest.explain: About 30% of PCD cases have normal TEM, so nasal NO, video microscopy and genetics are needed.

advancedTest.q: Why does failed nodal ciliary flow produce situs inversus in only about half of PCD patients?
choices: Nodal cilia are 9+2, so they are partly spared
Without leftward flow, left-right sidedness is set at random
Maternal dynein compensates in about half of embryos
Primary cilia restore flow in about half of patients
advancedTest.explain: With no directional cue from the 9+0 motile nodal cilia, laterality is determined at random.

advancedTest.q: A SHH-subgroup medulloblastoma resists Smoothened inhibition. The most consistent explanation is:
choices: Loss of tip-link proteins in the tumour cells
Upregulation of villin in the tumour's microvilli
Excess dynein activity speeding up the ciliary beat
A pathway mutation downstream of Smoothened
advancedTest.explain: Mutations downstream of Smoothened, such as in GLI-level components, keep the pathway active and bypass a Smoothened blockade.

advancedTest.q: Why might hair-cell stereocilia damage be poorly reversible compared with brush-border microvilli?
choices: Microvilli contain dynein motors that can self-repair
Stereociliary actin turns over slowly in long-lived, non-dividing cells
Stereocilia lack the cadherin-based tip links found on microvilli
Stereocilia rely on microtubules, which depolymerize when damaged
advancedTest.explain: Stereocilia are actin-based with very slow turnover in hair cells that do not renew, while enterocytes are constantly replaced.

lessons.title: Cell Junctions & the Basement Membrane

levels.kid:
Think of a brick wall. The bricks are cells, and the wall is a lining, like the inside of your tummy or the outside of your skin.

A good wall needs three things. First, **seals** between the bricks so water can't leak through the cracks. Second, **rivets** that hold the bricks tightly together so the wall doesn't fall apart when you pull on it. Third, **little tunnels** so neighbouring bricks can pass tiny messages to each other.

Cells have all three! They are called **junctions**.

Under the whole wall is a thin, strong mat called the **basement membrane**. The cells stand on it like a carpet glued to the floor. It holds them in place and keeps them in the right order.
levels.hs:
Epithelial cells sit packed side by side, forming sheets that line surfaces. To work as a barrier, they need **cell junctions**, which are special protein connections between neighbouring cells.

There are three main jobs, so there are three main kinds:
- **Tight junctions (occluding junctions)** seal the gap between cells near the top surface. They stop substances from leaking between cells, so material has to pass *through* the cells instead.
- **Anchoring junctions** link cells mechanically. **Adherens junctions** connect to the cell's actin filaments. **Desmosomes** act like spot welds, connected to tough intermediate filaments called **keratins**.
- **Gap junctions** are tiny channels that let ions and small molecules pass directly from one cell to the next, so cells can share signals.

Underneath every epithelium is the **basement membrane**, a thin sheet of protein that attaches the epithelium to the connective tissue below. Epithelium has no blood vessels of its own, so nutrients must diffuse across this sheet. Cells attach to it with **hemidesmosomes**, which are like half a desmosome.

Real example: in the blistering disease **pemphigus vulgaris**, the immune system attacks desmosome proteins in the skin. Skin cells come apart from each other and fragile blisters form, showing just how much these junctions matter.
levels.college:
Lateral and basal surfaces of epithelial cells carry junctions that are often found in a predictable top-to-bottom order called the **junctional complex**. Older light microscopists saw it as a dark line called the "terminal bar."

**1. Zonula occludens (tight junction).** It is the most apical junction. Rows of transmembrane proteins, **claudins** and **occludin**, form branching sealing strands that fuse adjacent membranes. They are anchored by scaffold proteins **ZO-1/2/3**. Tight junctions have two jobs:
- **Barrier function**: they control the **paracellular pathway**. Claudin types decide how leaky and how ion-selective the seal is.
- **Fence function**: they stop membrane proteins from drifting between the apical and basolateral domains, which maintains **polarity**.

**2. Zonula adherens.** It is a continuous belt just below the tight junction. **E-cadherin** binds in a calcium-dependent way to cadherin on the neighbouring cell. Inside the cell, **β-catenin** and **α-catenin** link it to a ring of actin.

**3. Macula adherens (desmosome).** These are spot-like plaques. The desmosomal cadherins **desmoglein** and **desmocollin** bind across the gap. **Plakoglobin**, **plakophilin** and **desmoplakin** form a dense plaque that anchors **keratin intermediate filaments**. Desmosomes spread mechanical stress across a sheet.

**4. Gap junctions.** Six **connexins** form a **connexon** (hemichannel). Connexons on neighbouring cells dock to form channels that pass molecules smaller than about 1 kDa, such as ions, cAMP and IP3.

On the basal side:
- **Hemidesmosomes** use **integrin α6β4** and **BP180** (collagen XVII) to link keratins to the basement membrane.
- **Focal adhesions** use other integrins to link actin to the matrix.

On electron microscopy, the **basal lamina** has two layers: a pale **lamina lucida** and a dense **lamina densa**, made of **type IV collagen**, **laminin**, **nidogen** and **perlecan**. Beneath it lies the **lamina reticularis**, made of reticular fibres (type III collagen) produced by connective tissue. Together these layers form the light-microscopic **basement membrane**, which stains well with **PAS**.
levels.phd:
Tight junction strands appear as anastomosing ridges on **freeze-fracture** electron microscopy. Claudins (more than 20 family members) are tetraspan proteins whose extracellular loops set the charge and size selectivity of the paracellular pathway. **Claudin-2** forms cation- and water-permeable pores in leaky epithelia such as the proximal tubule. **Claudin-16/19** mediate paracellular Mg²⁺ and Ca²⁺ reabsorption in the thick ascending limb. **Claudin-1** knockout mice die soon after birth from transepidermal water loss.

The paracellular pathway has two routes:
- A high-capacity **pore pathway**, made by claudins, that is charge- and size-selective (about 4 Å).
- A low-capacity **leak pathway** that lets larger solutes through and is regulated by ZO-1, occludin and **myosin light-chain kinase**-driven perijunctional actomyosin contraction.

Epithelial "tightness" is quantified by **transepithelial electrical resistance (TER)**. It ranges from tens of Ω·cm² in proximal tubule to thousands in urinary bladder. Strand number correlates only loosely with TER. Claudin composition matters more.

Adherens junctions are mechanosensors. Under tension, α-catenin unfolds and recruits **vinculin**, which strengthens the junction in a catch-bond manner. β-catenin moonlights in **Wnt signalling**, so cadherin loss can free it for transcription. Loss of E-cadherin (CDH1) is a hallmark of **epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT)**. Germline CDH1 mutations cause hereditary diffuse gastric cancer and lobular breast cancer.

Desmosomes can become **hyperadhesive**, a calcium-independent state typical of mature tissue. The cadherin extracellular domains interdigitate to form the dense midline seen on electron microscopy.

Basal lamina assembly is nucleated by **laminin** trimers (for example laminin-332 in skin, laminin-511 widely). Laminin polymerises at the cell surface through integrin and dystroglycan binding. A separate **collagen IV** network, stabilised by **sulfilimine** cross-links made by **peroxidasin**, is then bridged to it by nidogen and perlecan. Basement membranes are therefore cell-instructive scaffolds, not inert glue.
levels.expert:
Junction and basement membrane defects produce a coherent clinical map. That map is diagnostically useful because **immunofluorescence (IF)** pattern localises the target.

**Autoimmune blistering disease:**
- **Pemphigus vulgaris** targets desmoglein 3 (mucosal) with or without desmoglein 1. It causes **suprabasal acantholysis**, with basal cells left as a "tombstone row." Direct IF shows intercellular "chicken-wire" IgG.
- **Pemphigus foliaceus** targets desmoglein 1 and splits the skin superficially. The **desmoglein compensation** hypothesis explains why the split level follows the antibody profile and where each desmoglein is expressed.
- Staphylococcal **exfoliative toxins** are serine proteases that cleave desmoglein 1. This explains staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, which reproduces pemphigus foliaceus histology without antibodies.
- **Bullous pemphigoid** targets BP180 and BP230 and causes a subepidermal split. Direct IF shows linear IgG/C3 along the basement membrane zone. On **salt-split skin**, staining lands on the blister roof. In epidermolysis bullosa acquisita (anti-collagen VII), staining lands on the floor.
- **Anti-GBM (Goodpasture) disease** targets the NC1 domain of the α3 chain of collagen IV and gives linear glomerular IgG. **Alport syndrome**, caused by COL4A3/4/5 mutations, gives a split, laminated GBM on electron microscopy.

**Inherited disease:**
- **Epidermolysis bullosa** subtypes map onto the layers: keratin 5/14 (simplex), laminin-332 or collagen XVII (junctional), collagen VII anchoring fibrils (dystrophic).
- Desmosomal mutations in **plakophilin-2** and **desmoplakin** cause **arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy**. Cardiac **intercalated discs** share desmosomal machinery.
- **Connexin 26 (GJB2)** mutations are the commonest cause of inherited nonsyndromic deafness. **Connexin 32** mutations cause X-linked Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease.
- **Claudin-16/19** mutations cause familial hypomagnesaemia with hypercalciuria.

**Pharmacology angle:**
- *Clostridium perfringens* enterotoxin binds claudin-3/4. Its C-terminal fragment is used experimentally to open barriers.
- Barrier-opening strategies are being explored to improve drug delivery across epithelia.
- The neurosurgical analogue is the **blood-brain barrier**, where endothelial tight junctions rich in claudin-5 are the main obstacle to CNS drug delivery. Transient disruption with focused ultrasound plus microbubbles is now in clinical trials.

**Pitfall:** in tumours, a breached basement membrane on collagen IV or laminin immunostaining is what separates in situ from invasive carcinoma. Tangential sectioning can mimic breaches, so always read basal lamina continuity against section orientation.

keyPoints: Tight junctions (claudins, occludin) seal the paracellular pathway and fence apical from basolateral membrane
Adherens junctions use E-cadherin and catenins to link actin belts between cells
Desmosomes use desmogleins and desmocollins to anchor keratin filaments
Gap junctions are connexin channels passing small molecules under about 1 kDa
Hemidesmosomes (integrin α6β4, BP180) attach cells to the basal lamina
Basal lamina = type IV collagen, laminin, nidogen, perlecan; plus lamina reticularis = basement membrane

test.q: Which junction seals the space between neighbouring epithelial cells?
test.explain: Tight junctions (zonula occludens) close the paracellular route. Desmosomes provide strength, not a seal.

test.q: Desmosomes anchor which cytoskeletal element?
test.explain: Desmoplakin links desmosomes to keratin intermediate filaments. Adherens junctions link to actin instead.

test.q: Gap junction channels are built from proteins called:
test.explain: Six connexins form a connexon, and two docked connexons form the channel.

test.q: Which protein is the main adhesion molecule of the zonula adherens?
test.explain: E-cadherin binds in a calcium-dependent way and links to actin through catenins. Desmoglein belongs to desmosomes.

test.q: Which collagen type forms the network of the lamina densa?
test.explain: Type IV collagen forms a sheet-like network. Type III forms the reticular fibres of the lamina reticularis.

test.q: The 'fence function' of tight junctions helps cells to:
choices: Move cilia in a coordinated wave
Grip the basement membrane during stretching
Pass ions directly into a neighbouring cell
Keep apical and basolateral membrane proteins apart
test.explain: By blocking lateral diffusion in the membrane, tight junctions maintain cell polarity.

test.q: In pemphigus vulgaris, autoantibodies attack:
test.explain: Pemphigus targets desmogleins, so keratinocytes separate from each other and blisters form.

test.q: What is the usual top-to-bottom order of the junctional complex?
test.explain: The zonula occludens is most apical, then the zonula adherens, then the macula adherens (desmosome).

test.q: Which stain highlights the basement membrane well by light microscopy?
test.explain: The carbohydrate-rich glycoproteins of the basement membrane are PAS-positive.

test.q: Cells attach to the basal lamina with ___, which resemble half a desmosome.
test.explain: Hemidesmosomes use integrin α6β4 and BP180 to anchor keratins to the basal lamina.

test.q: Which family of tetraspan proteins sets how leaky and ion-selective a tight junction is?
test.explain: Different claudin types (for example claudin-2 in proximal tubule) set the selectivity of the paracellular pathway.

test.q: The route for substances passing between cells, rather than through them, is the ___ pathway.
test.explain: Tight junctions regulate the paracellular pathway. The route through the cells is called transcellular.

kidTest.q: What do tight junctions do?
kidTest.explain: They work like seals so water can't leak through the cracks.

kidTest.q: Desmosomes are like:
kidTest.explain: They hold cells tightly so the sheet doesn't pull apart.

kidTest.q: What do gap junctions let cells do?
kidTest.explain: They are little tunnels between neighbouring cells.

kidTest.q: Where is the basement membrane?
kidTest.explain: It is a thin mat the cells stand on, like a carpet.

kidTest.q: The connections between cells are called j _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Junctions seal, hold and connect cells.

advancedTest.q: A biopsy shows a suprabasal split with basal cells left attached like a 'tombstone row'. Which IF pattern fits best?
choices: Linear IgG along the basement membrane zone
Granular IgA at dermal papillary tips
Linear IgG on the floor of salt-split skin
advancedTest.explain: Suprabasal acantholysis means pemphigus vulgaris, where anti-desmoglein IgG outlines cells. Linear basement membrane staining fits pemphigoid.

advancedTest.q: Two epithelia have the same number of tight junction strands but very different TER. The best explanation is a difference in:
choices: Claudin isoform composition of the strands
Basal lamina thickness under each epithelium
advancedTest.explain: TER tracks claudin type more than strand number. Pore-forming claudins such as claudin-2 make an epithelium leaky.

advancedTest.q: Why can loss of E-cadherin promote invasive tumour behaviour beyond simple loss of adhesion?
choices: It frees β-catenin to join Wnt-driven transcription
It thickens the lamina densa around tumour nests
It blocks connexons from carrying growth signals
It converts desmosomes to a hyperadhesive state
advancedTest.explain: β-catenin links cadherin to actin and also acts in Wnt signalling. Cadherin loss supports EMT both mechanically and through signalling.

advancedTest.q: On salt-split skin, linear IgG stains the blister floor. Which target is most consistent?
choices: Collagen VII in the anchoring fibrils
advancedTest.explain: Collagen VII sits below the split, so antibodies against it (EBA) stain the floor. BP180 antibodies stain the roof.

lessons.title: Exocrine Glands & Modes of Secretion

levels.kid:
Some cells in your body are tiny factories. They make useful juices, like spit, sweat and tears. Groups of these factory cells are called **glands**.

Some glands send their juice through a little pipe, called a **duct**, out onto your skin or into your tummy. These are **exocrine glands**. Your sweat glands and spit glands are exocrine glands.

Glands can let their juice out in different ways:
- Some pack it in tiny bubbles and pop them open at the edge of the cell.
- Some pinch off a little piece of the cell along with the juice.
- Some fill up with juice and then the whole cell breaks open, like a water balloon.

New cells grow to replace the ones that burst.
levels.hs:
A **gland** is a group of epithelial cells specialized to make and release a product. Glands form when surface epithelium grows down into the tissue underneath.

**Exocrine glands** keep a connection to the surface, a tube called a **duct**, and release their product onto a surface or into a cavity. Examples are sweat, salivary and mammary glands. **Endocrine glands** lose the duct and release hormones into the blood. They are covered in a later unit.

Exocrine glands are described in two main ways:
- **Structure**: a **simple** gland has one unbranched duct, and a **compound** gland has a branched duct. The secretory end can be a **tubule** (a tube shape) or an **acinus** (a round, grape-like sac).
- **Product**: **serous** cells make a watery, enzyme-rich fluid. **Mucous** cells make thick, slippery mucus.

There are also three **modes of secretion**:
- **Merocrine**: the product leaves in vesicles by exocytosis, and the cell stays intact. Most glands work this way.
- **Apocrine**: the top of the cell pinches off with the product.
- **Holocrine**: the whole cell fills with product and dies, breaking apart. Sebaceous (oil) glands in the skin work like this.

A real example: the **goblet cell** in your intestine is a gland made of a single cell. It releases mucus that protects the lining.
levels.college:
Glands form when epithelium grows down into the underlying connective tissue. In **exocrine** glands, the cord of cells that links the gland to the surface hollows out into a duct. In **endocrine** glands, that cord disappears and the gland releases its product into nearby capillaries.

**Classification of exocrine glands**
- **Cell number**: unicellular (the **goblet cell**) or multicellular.
- **Duct branching**: simple (an unbranched duct) or compound (a branched duct).
- **Secretory unit shape**: tubular, coiled tubular (eccrine sweat gland), acinar/alveolar, or tubuloacinar.
- Examples: simple tubular (intestinal crypts), simple branched acinar (sebaceous gland), compound tubuloacinar (submandibular gland, exocrine pancreas).

**Secretory product**
- **Serous** cells: pyramidal, with a round basal nucleus and strong basal basophilia from abundant rough ER. They have apical eosinophilic **zymogen granules** and make watery fluid containing enzymes. Examples are the parotid gland and pancreatic acini.
- **Mucous** cells: pale, foamy cytoplasm on H&E, because the mucin is washed out during processing. The nucleus is flattened against the base, and the cells stain strongly with **PAS**.
- **Mixed** glands: in the submandibular gland, serous cells form **serous demilunes** that cap mucous tubules. Part of this crescent shape is a fixation artifact.

**Modes of secretion**
- **Merocrine (eccrine)**: exocytosis of vesicles, with no loss of cytoplasm. Seen in salivary glands, pancreas and eccrine sweat glands.
- **Apocrine**: the product leaves with a rim of apical cytoplasm wrapped in membrane. The lipid droplets of milk in the mammary gland are the classic example.
- **Holocrine**: the whole cell matures, fills with product and disintegrates. In the sebaceous gland, basal stem cells replace the lost cells.

**Myoepithelial cells**: contractile epithelial cells that sit between the secretory cells and the basal lamina. They squeeze acini and ducts. In the mammary gland they respond to oxytocin.

**Ducts** in large glands go from intercalated ducts to striated ducts, then to interlobular ducts. Striated ducts change the composition of the fluid.
levels.phd:
Merocrine secretion splits into two pathways. In **regulated secretion**, cargo is condensed in the trans-Golgi network into dense-core granules. In acinar cells these appear as zymogen granules, held near the apical membrane by cortical actin. When a stimulus raises intracellular Ca²⁺, fusion is driven by **SNARE** complexes (VAMP2/8, syntaxin, SNAP-23) with Munc18 and synaptotagmin. In the pancreas the stimuli are CCK and acetylcholine acting through Gq-coupled receptors. **Constitutive secretion** runs continuously. George Palade's pulse-chase autoradiography of guinea-pig pancreatic acinar cells traced the route rough ER → Golgi → condensing vacuole → granule → lumen. That work earned the 1974 Nobel Prize, and it established the secretory pathway for every eukaryotic cell.

**Primary versus final secretion.** In salivary glands, acini produce an isotonic, plasma-like primary fluid. Cl⁻ exits apically through **TMEM16A** channels, with NKCC1 loading Cl⁻ basolaterally, and water follows through **aquaporin-5**. **Striated ducts**, whose basal infoldings are packed with mitochondria to power Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, then reabsorb Na⁺ and Cl⁻ and secrete K⁺ and HCO₃⁻. Because the ducts are poorly permeable to water, the final saliva is **hypotonic**. Pancreatic ducts do the reverse kind of modification: they add HCO₃⁻ through CFTR and SLC26A6.

**Apocrine secretion revisited.** Electron microscopy shows that the human axillary "apocrine" sweat gland releases most of its protein by merocrine exocytosis, and apical blebbing makes up only a small part. In the mammary gland, apocrine release is real: lipid droplets are wrapped in apical plasma membrane, forming the milk fat globule membrane. That membrane includes butyrophilin and xanthine oxidoreductase. Some authors argue that "apocrine" describes an appearance rather than a single mechanism. Proteomic studies show apocrine-type release of leaderless proteins in several tissues.

**Holocrine secretion** in the sebaceous gland is a programmed form of terminal differentiation. Lipogenic sebocytes build up triglycerides, wax esters and squalene, then die by a process distinct from classic apoptosis, involving DNase2-dependent nuclear breakdown. This depends on renewal by Blimp1⁺/Lrig1⁺ progenitors.
levels.expert:
Glands matter clinically because so many diseases hit one of the steps just described.

- **Cystic fibrosis**: CFTR dysfunction impairs Cl⁻/HCO₃⁻ secretion in pancreatic ducts. Protein-rich, acidic secretions plug the ducts, leading to autodigestion and exocrine pancreatic insufficiency. In sweat glands the defect is in the duct, not the coil. NaCl cannot be reabsorbed, which is the basis of the **sweat chloride test**. CFTR modulators such as elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor lower sweat chloride, and in young children may partly preserve pancreatic function.
- **Sjögren disease**: lymphocytic infiltration of salivary and lacrimal glands. Minor labial salivary gland biopsy is scored by **focus score** (≥1 focus of ≥50 lymphocytes per 4 mm²). Studies have reported altered aquaporin-5 localization and anti-muscarinic M3 antibodies. Muscarinic agonists (pilocarpine, cevimeline) stimulate the remaining acini.
- **Sebaceous glands**: androgens drive sebocyte proliferation in acne. Isotretinoin markedly shrinks the glands; it is teratogenic and needs strict pregnancy prevention. Muir-Torre syndrome, a Lynch variant, presents with sebaceous neoplasms.
- **Pancreatitis**: premature intracellular trypsinogen activation, partly through cathepsin B co-localization, together with blocked apical exocytosis, redirects zymogen release basolaterally. This is a classic experimental model (cerulein hyperstimulation).

**Myoepithelial cells** have diagnostic value in pathology. In breast, an intact p63/SMMHC/calponin-positive myoepithelial layer distinguishes in situ or benign lesions from invasive carcinoma. Salivary gland tumors often contain both ductal and myoepithelial cells. Pleomorphic adenoma (PLAG1/HMGA2 fusions) is the most common salivary tumor, and adenoid cystic carcinoma (MYB-NFIB) is known for perineural invasion. That makes it relevant to skull-base surgeons, since it can track along cranial nerves V and VII.

**Research frontiers**:
- Salivary gland organoids and Kit⁺ progenitor transplantation aim to restore function after head-and-neck radiotherapy.
- Single-cell atlases have redefined ductal heterogeneity, including the ionocyte-like cells of salivary ducts.
- The pancreatic ductal epithelium is under study for acinar-to-ductal metaplasia as an early step in pancreatic cancer.

A common pitfall when reading slides is mistaking artifact-pale mucous cells for vacuolated or degenerating cells.

keyPoints: Exocrine glands release products through ducts; endocrine glands release hormones into blood
Glands are classified by duct branching (simple/compound) and secretory unit shape (tubular/acinar)
Serous cells make watery enzyme fluid; mucous cells make PAS-positive mucus
Merocrine = exocytosis, apocrine = apical cytoplasm lost, holocrine = whole cell disintegrates
Myoepithelial cells contract to squeeze secretions out
Ducts modify the primary secretion, as striated ducts do in saliva

test.q: What distinguishes an exocrine gland from an endocrine gland?
choices: It releases hormones into nearby capillaries
It releases its product through a duct
It is built from muscle, not epithelium
It forms from connective tissue cells
test.explain: Exocrine glands keep a duct connection to a surface or cavity. Endocrine glands are ductless and secrete into blood.

test.q: Sebaceous glands release their oily product by which mode?
test.explain: In holocrine secretion the whole cell fills with lipid and disintegrates, which is how sebaceous glands work.

test.q: Merocrine secretion involves:
choices: Loss of a rim of apical cytoplasm
Release of hormones into lymph vessels
Exocytosis of vesicles from an intact cell
Rupture and death of the whole cell
test.explain: Merocrine cells release product by exocytosis and lose no cytoplasm. This is the most common mode.

test.q: The lipid droplets of milk are a classic example of which secretion mode?
test.explain: Milk lipid leaves wrapped in apical membrane and a little cytoplasm, which is apocrine secretion.

test.q: On H&E, mucous cells typically look:
choices: Bright red with many large granules
Pale and foamy with a flat basal nucleus
Dark with a round central nucleus
test.explain: Mucin washes out during processing, leaving pale, foamy cells with a nucleus flattened against the base.

test.q: A gland with a branched duct is called:
test.explain: Compound glands have branched ducts. Simple glands have a single unbranched duct.

test.q: What is the main job of myoepithelial cells?
choices: Absorbing sodium from the duct lumen
test.explain: Myoepithelial cells are contractile and push secretions out of acini and ducts.

test.q: Which is an example of a unicellular exocrine gland?
test.explain: The goblet cell is a single mucus-secreting cell, which counts as a gland on its own.

test.q: Serous cells show strong basal basophilia mainly because of abundant:
test.explain: Rough ER ribosomes stain blue (basophilic) and support enzyme protein synthesis.

test.q: A round, grape-like secretory unit of a gland is called an ___.
test.explain: Acinar (alveolar) units are sac-shaped, unlike tubular units.

test.q: Which stain turns mucous cells strongly magenta?
test.explain: PAS stains carbohydrate-rich mucins strongly.

test.q: In the submandibular gland, serous cells capping mucous tubules form serous ___.
test.explain: Serous demilunes are crescent-shaped caps, partly a fixation artifact.

kidTest.q: What is a gland?
choices: A small bone inside the ear
A group of cells that make a juice
kidTest.explain: Glands are groups of cells that make useful juices like spit and sweat.

kidTest.q: Which of these comes from an exocrine gland?
kidTest.explain: Sweat glands send sweat through a little pipe onto the skin.

kidTest.q: In one kind of gland, the whole cell breaks open. What is it like?
kidTest.explain: Holocrine cells fill up and burst, like a water balloon.

kidTest.q: What happens after cells burst open?
choices: New cells grow to replace them
kidTest.explain: New cells grow and take their place.

kidTest.q: The little pipe a gland uses is called a d _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: A duct carries the juice out of the gland.

advancedTest.q: Saliva ends up hypotonic even though the acinar fluid is isotonic. Why?
choices: Myoepithelial cells filter out ions during each contraction
Acini secrete extra water through aquaporin-5 channels
Ducts reabsorb NaCl but are poorly permeable to water
Holocrine breakdown of duct cells dilutes the fluid
advancedTest.explain: Duct cells pull out Na⁺ and Cl⁻, but water cannot follow, so the final fluid is hypotonic. Aquaporin-5 acts in the acini, where the fluid is still isotonic.

advancedTest.q: In cystic fibrosis, sweat chloride is high mainly because:
choices: The secretory coil overproduces chloride-rich fluid
Apocrine glands replace eccrine sweat glands
Ductal CFTR fails to reabsorb chloride
advancedTest.explain: The defect is in reabsorption in the duct, not secretion in the coil, so NaCl stays in the sweat.

advancedTest.q: Why is the label 'apocrine' for human axillary sweat glands controversial?
choices: They have no duct opening onto the surface of the skin
EM shows most protein leaves by merocrine exocytosis
Their product is released directly into capillaries
They secrete by holocrine death of the whole cell
advancedTest.explain: Electron microscopy shows apical blebbing is a small part of their output. Most protein leaves by exocytosis.

advancedTest.q: A breast lesion shows an intact p63-positive layer around the ducts. This most supports:
choices: Loss of serous demilunes in the gland
An in situ or benign lesion with myoepithelium preserved
Invasive carcinoma breaching the basal lamina
advancedTest.explain: A preserved myoepithelial layer argues against invasion, because invasive carcinoma loses it.

lessons.title: Epithelial Renewal, Stem Cells & Metaplasia

levels.kid:
Your skin and the inside of your tummy are covered by thin sheets of cells called **epithelium**. These sheets get rubbed, scraped and worn out all the time. So your body keeps making new ones!

Deep down, at the bottom of each sheet, live special helper cells called **stem cells**. They are like a bakery that never closes. They keep making fresh cells, and the new cells slowly move up to replace the old ones on top.

The lining of your gut is replaced about every 4 to 5 days. Your skin's outer layer takes about a month.

Sometimes, if a place keeps getting hurt, like a smoker's airway, the body swaps in a tougher kind of cell. This swap is called **metaplasia**. It is like trading a soft carpet for tough tiles.
levels.hs:
Epithelia line surfaces that face constant wear: skin, gut, airways. To survive, they must keep replacing lost cells. This is **epithelial renewal**, and it depends on **stem cells**.

A stem cell can do two things:
- **Self-renew**: divide to make more stem cells.
- **Differentiate**: produce cells that mature into specialized types.

Often a stem cell first makes **transit-amplifying cells**, which divide quickly a few times to multiply the numbers before they mature.

Where stem cells live depends on the tissue:
- In skin, they sit in the **basal layer** (stratum basale) and in the hair follicle bulge. New keratinocytes rise to the surface and are shed after roughly 4 weeks.
- In the small intestine, they sit at the bottom of the **crypts**. New cells climb up the villi and are shed at the tip in about 3 to 5 days, one of the fastest turnover rates in the body.

**Metaplasia** is when one mature cell type is replaced by another that copes better with stress. It is usually reversible if the stress stops. Real example: in smokers, the ciliated **pseudostratified columnar** epithelium of the bronchi can become **stratified squamous** epithelium. It is tougher, but it loses the cilia and mucus that clear particles, and metaplastic areas can be a step on the road to cancer.
levels.college:
Epithelial tissues are classified by renewal behavior into fast-renewing (intestine, epidermis, cornea), slowly renewing (liver, kidney tubules, which proliferate mainly after injury) and essentially static populations. Renewal follows a **hierarchy**: stem cell → transit-amplifying (TA) progenitor → terminally differentiated cell.

**Key stem cell niches:**
- **Small intestine**: **Lgr5+ crypt base columnar cells** sit between Paneth cells at the crypt base. TA cells divide in the lower crypt, then differentiate into enterocytes, goblet, enteroendocrine and tuft cells as they migrate up the villus. Paneth cells move downward and live weeks.
- **Epidermis**: basal keratinocytes on the basement membrane divide. Daughters move through the spinosum, granulosum and corneum. Hair follicle **bulge** stem cells help repair wounds.
- **Cornea**: **limbal stem cells** at the corneoscleral junction.
- **Airway**: **basal cells** of the pseudostratified epithelium; club cells in bronchioles.

**Niche signals** keep stem cells in their state. **Wnt** is highest at the crypt base and is supplied partly by Paneth cells and mesenchyme. Notch signaling biases cells toward absorptive or secretory fates. BMP rises toward the villus and promotes differentiation.

**Metaplasia** is a reversible switch of one differentiated epithelial type for another. It arises from reprogramming of stem or progenitor cells, not from mature cells changing shape. Classic examples:
- **Squamous metaplasia** of bronchi (smoking) or of the endocervix at the transformation zone.
- **Barrett esophagus**: stratified squamous epithelium is replaced by intestinal-type columnar epithelium with goblet cells, driven by acid and bile reflux.
- Intestinal metaplasia of the stomach (often after *H. pylori* gastritis).

Metaplasia is adaptive but costly. Lost function (cilia, mucus) and a sustained proliferative stimulus raise the risk of **dysplasia** and carcinoma, such as esophageal adenocarcinoma arising in Barrett mucosa.
levels.phd:
Two influential models of epithelial stem cell behavior have been revised by lineage tracing. In the intestine, Barker, Clevers et al. (2007) used Lgr5-EGFP-IRES-CreERT2 mice to show that Lgr5+ crypt base columnar (CBC) cells generate all epithelial lineages for long periods. Snippert et al. (2010) used Confetti multicolor tracing and found that each crypt drifts to **monoclonality** through **neutral competition**: roughly 14–16 equipotent stem cells divide symmetrically, and clones are lost or fixed at random. This replaced strict asymmetric-division models. The older '+4' label-retaining cell (Potten) is now viewed partly as secretory progenitors capable of dedifferentiation.

**Plasticity** is central. After Lgr5+ cell ablation (diphtheria toxin receptor models) or irradiation, crypts regenerate from committed secretory and enterocyte progenitors and from revival-like states (Clu+ cells, Ayyaz et al. 2019) that are YAP-dependent. Stemness therefore behaves as a niche-conferred state rather than a fixed identity. Niche components include Paneth-derived Wnt3, EGF and Dll1/4, plus mesenchymal R-spondin and Grem1. Sato et al. (2009) translated this into **organoids**: single Lgr5+ cells grown in Matrigel with EGF, Noggin and R-spondin form self-organizing crypt-villus units.

In epidermis, Clayton et al. (2007) proposed a single committed-progenitor population with stochastic fate choices (balanced overall). This sparked debate with hierarchical models that include slow-cycling stem cells; the evidence now differs by body site.

Metaplasia mechanisms involve transcription factor switches. Barrett mucosa expresses **CDX1/CDX2** and SOX9. Its cell of origin is contested: candidates include squamous basal cells, submucosal gland ducts, residual embryonic cells at the squamocolumnar junction (Wang et al. 2011), and gastric cardia progenitors pushed up by Il1b-driven inflammation (Quante et al. 2012). Gastric **SPEM** (spasmolytic polypeptide-expressing metaplasia, TFF2+) arises in part from chief-cell reprogramming via 'paligenosis' (Mills), illustrating that differentiated cells can re-enter the cycle.
levels.expert:
Clinically, the stem cell biology above explains why fast-renewing epithelia are the main sites of toxicity from cytotoxic chemotherapy and radiation. Mucositis, diarrhea and alopecia reflect ablation of transit-amplifying compartments. Radiation enteropathy correlates with crypt stem cell survival, measured classically with the Withers microcolony assay. Recovery depends on plastic progenitors, which links mechanistic work to radioprotection strategies.

**Barrett esophagus in practice:**
- Diagnosis requires endoscopic columnar mucosa at least 1 cm above the gastroesophageal junction. US guidelines also require intestinal metaplasia with goblet cells on biopsy; British guidelines do not.
- The Prague C&M criteria record extent. Biopsy follows the Seattle protocol: four-quadrant samples at regular intervals.
- Progression risk for non-dysplastic Barrett is low, roughly 0.2–0.5% per year, which drives debate over surveillance cost. Dysplasia is reviewed by an expert pathologist because interobserver agreement for low-grade dysplasia is poor.
- Dysplastic Barrett is managed with endoscopic resection plus radiofrequency ablation. The squamous epithelium that regrows is called neosquamous epithelium. Buried glands beneath it are a pitfall.
- Molecular tools are emerging: TP53 immunostaining, the Cytosponge-TFF3 swallowed sampling device, and tissue systems-pathology tests.

**Pathology pitfalls:** pseudogoblet cells (distended foveolar cells) can mimic intestinal metaplasia. Reactive atypia in inflamed or regenerating epithelium mimics dysplasia, so maturation toward the surface is a key reassuring feature. The cervical transformation zone is where HPV preferentially infects reserve cells undergoing squamous metaplasia. This is why cytology sampling targets it.

**Field cancerization** (Slaughter 1953) reflects the same stem cell dynamics. Mutant clones, such as NOTCH1 and TP53 clones in normal-appearing esophagus (Martincorena et al. 2018), spread through neutral or biased competition across large areas of mucosa. Most of these clones never become cancer, which challenges simple mutation-based risk models.

**Regenerative translation:** cultured limbal stem cell grafts (Holoclar, EU-approved) treat limbal stem cell deficiency after chemical burns. Graft success depends on p63-bright holoclone content. Transgenic epidermal stem cell grafts regenerated most of the skin of a child with junctional epidermolysis bullosa (Hirsch et al. 2017).

Open questions: what triggers dedifferentiation in humans, and can metaplasia be reversed pharmacologically?

keyPoints: Wear-exposed epithelia renew continuously from stem cells
Hierarchy: stem cell → transit-amplifying cell → differentiated cell
Intestinal Lgr5+ stem cells sit in crypt bases; epidermal stem cells in the basal layer and follicle bulge
Niche signals (Wnt, Notch, BMP) control stemness and fate
Metaplasia is a reversible switch of one mature epithelium for another
Metaplasia (e.g. Barrett esophagus) can progress to dysplasia and cancer

test.q: Which two abilities define a stem cell?
test.explain: Stem cells make more of themselves and also produce cells that specialize.

test.q: Where are intestinal epithelial stem cells located?
test.explain: Lgr5+ stem cells sit at the bottom of crypts, and new cells migrate up toward the villus tips.

test.q: Approximately how long does small intestinal epithelium take to turn over?
test.explain: The small intestine renews in days. About 4 weeks fits the epidermis.

test.q: What role do transit-amplifying cells play?
choices: They anchor cells to the basement membrane
They divide rapidly to expand cell numbers
They form tight junctions between cells
They secrete Wnt to the niche
test.explain: TA cells undergo a few rapid divisions before they differentiate.

test.q: Smoking can change bronchial pseudostratified columnar epithelium into which type?
test.explain: This is squamous metaplasia. The new epithelium is tougher but lacks cilia.

test.q: Barrett esophagus replaces squamous epithelium with what?
test.explain: Reflux drives a switch to columnar epithelium with goblet cells.

test.q: Which signal is strongest at the crypt base and maintains stemness?
test.explain: Wnt is concentrated at the crypt base. BMP rises toward the villus and promotes differentiation.

test.q: Metaplasia is best described as which of these?
choices: A reversible change of cell type
test.explain: Metaplasia swaps one mature cell type for another and usually reverses when the stress stops.

test.q: Where are corneal epithelial stem cells found?
test.explain: Limbal stem cells sit at the corneoscleral junction.

test.q: In skin, epidermal stem cells sit in the stratum ___.
test.explain: The basal layer rests on the basement membrane and divides.

test.q: What term describes abnormal, precancerous growth that can follow metaplasia?
test.explain: Metaplasia can progress to dysplasia and then carcinoma.

test.q: Hair follicle stem cells that help repair wounds live in the follicle ___.
test.explain: Bulge stem cells contribute to wound repair of the epidermis.

kidTest.q: What do stem cells do?
kidTest.explain: Stem cells keep making fresh cells.

kidTest.q: Where do skin stem cells live?
kidTest.explain: They live deep down at the bottom of the sheet.

kidTest.q: Which lining is replaced fastest?
kidTest.explain: The gut lining is replaced every few days.

kidTest.q: Why does the body swap in tougher cells?
kidTest.explain: Tougher cells help a place that is hurt again and again.

kidTest.q: What is the swap to a tougher cell type called? m _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _
kidTest.explain: Metaplasia means changing to a different kind of cell.

advancedTest.q: Confetti tracing showed crypts becoming monoclonal over time. What best explains this?
choices: Fusion of neighbouring crypts into one unit
Selective death of Paneth cells at the crypt base
Neutral competition among equipotent stem cells
Strict asymmetric division of a single stem cell
advancedTest.explain: Equal stem cells compete at random, so one clone eventually takes over each crypt by drift.

advancedTest.q: Crypts regenerate after Lgr5+ cells are ablated. What does this imply?
choices: Paneth cells are the true intestinal stem cells
Villus cells migrate down to form new crypts
Lgr5+ cells are not genuine stem cells
Stemness is a niche-conferred, plastic state
advancedTest.explain: Committed progenitors can dedifferentiate when the niche signals for it. Lineage tracing still shows Lgr5+ cells are genuine stem cells.

advancedTest.q: NOTCH1-mutant clones are common in normal esophagus. What does this challenge?
choices: The idea that renewal requires stem cells
Simple mutation-count models of cancer risk
The existence of basal cells in squamous epithelia
The role of reflux in Barrett esophagus
advancedTest.explain: Widespread clones rarely become cancer, so mutation counts alone predict risk poorly.

advancedTest.q: Why do mucositis and alopecia follow cytotoxic therapy?
choices: Selective loss of differentiated surface cells
Ablation of rapidly dividing TA compartments
advancedTest.explain: Fast-cycling transit-amplifying cells are most vulnerable to drugs that target dividing cells.
